THE CITY.—The Health Department now seizes watered milk in Brooklyn as in Manhattan, the boroughs being one city. The milkman says the cows were taking a tonic and are much improved.
THE AQUARIUM.—The new Aquarium in Castle Garden shows fishes of every kind to the public free. A druggist of the Battery sells a remedy for sea-sickness to those who come out looking pale.
THE SPRING TONICS.—The druggists of the ward have put the spring tonics in the window, the same bottles as last spring with the word SPRING on them. The ward is said to feel the difference.

standing: THE BLOOD.—Every proprietor of the ward now sells a remedy to purify the blood. Our reporter asked one what was the matter with the blood, and was told that he would know when he had bought a bottle.
THE GUARANTEE.—A proprietor of Canal street guarantees his remedy to cure or the money returned. The money has not been asked for, his customers either being cured or not being in a position to ask.
THE HERB DOCTOR.—An herb doctor of Christie street prescribes by looking at the tongue, and has been asked by the Board of Health to look at his license. He says the license is in his other coat.

THE CLAIRVOYANT.—A clairvoyant of Second avenue diagnoses by letter, at a dollar the letter. A proprietor of the ward has written to ask what she would recommend, and been told his own remedy, at the regular price.
THE DENTIST.—A painless dentist of the Bowery draws teeth to music, the band covering the patient. A druggist next door sells a remedy for the teeth that remain.
THE BEER.—The brewers of the city have raised the price of the pail, and the druggists of the ward report the sale of bitters, which are not beer, up by the same amount.

THE CORNER.—A man has stood at the corner of Grand street and the Bowery every day for a year, saying that the end of the world is at hand. A proprietor of the corner has asked him to add that a remedy is at hand also, and he has declined.

A LOST CHILD.—A child of four found wandering in Mulberry street was taken to the station house and claimed by four mothers before nightfall. The right one was found by the sergeant, who knew the smell of her remedy.
THE MIDWIVES.—The Board of Health asks the midwives of the ward to register. Several have replied that they are too busy, and one that she is a druggist.
A BIRTHDAY.—A woman of Cherry street kept her hundredth birthday on Sunday and attributed her years to never having taken a patent medicine. Three proprietors have since called to offer her one.

THE BOOTBLACKS.—The bootblacks of Park Row have formed a union and raised the price of a shine to six cents. A proprietor of a remedy for tired feet has given each boy a card to hand to his customers.

THE FIRE ESCAPES.—The inspectors report the fire-escapes of Elizabeth street so crowded with bedding, plants and bottles that a fireman could not get down them. The bottles, the inspectors say, were the hardest to move.

A DOG.—A dog of Baxter street has learned to fetch its master's remedy from the druggist's with the money in a basket. The druggist says it is his best customer, and the only one who never argues the price.
THE SCALES.—A penny weighing machine has been set up at the corner of Hester street, and the ward has found that it weighs more than it thought. A proprietor of an anti-fat remedy stands beside it.
A LECTURE.—A lecturer at Cooper Union spoke for two hours on the evils of patent medicines, and was interrupted by a cough, which a proprietor in the audience at once offered to cure.

standing.text: THE LETTER CARRIERS.—The letter carriers of the ward say that the heaviest mail of the year is the almanacs of the patent medicines, which come in January and are used for kindling in February.

standing: THE GARBAGE.—The garbage scows have been held at the dock for a week by the weather, and the ward has noticed. A druggist of Catharine street sells a remedy for the smell, which he says is the smell.

THE TENEMENT FIRE.—The tenants of a house in Monroe street who were brought down the ladders in their nightclothes on Tuesday say the first thing they saved was the rent book, and the second the remedy.

THE WIDOW'S PENSION.—A widow of Oliver street has been paid her pension by the Government after eleven years of letters. She has spent the first quarter on a remedy for the nerves the letters gave her.

standing.text: THE TYPE-WRITER.—A young lady type-writer in a Broadway office types sixty words a minute, and the gentlemen of the office are said to come in early to watch her. A druggist of the building sells a remedy for their nerves.
THE MISSION BAND.—A Salvation Army band has been playing on the Bowery, and was pelted. The bandsmen have asked the druggists of the street to sell them nothing for the bruises, wishing to bear them.
THE STATUE.—The pedestal on Bedloe's Island rises a course of granite a week. A proprietor of bitters, who once hoped to see the lady hold his bottle, now hopes only to see her from his roof.
THE MESSENGER BOYS.—The district messenger boys of Broadway have been timed by a gentleman with a watch and found to walk a mile in forty minutes. They say they are paid by the message, not the mile.

THE HACKMEN.—The hackmen at the Grand Central Depot charge a stranger a dollar to drive him round the block to the hotel opposite. The druggist on the corner sells the stranger a remedy for the shock.
THE PENNY PAPERS.—The newsboys now cry the Journal and the World at a cent apiece and fight over the corners. A proprietor of the ward advertises in both, and buys neither.
THE BIKE SHOPS.—A druggist of Third avenue has given over his front window to bicycle lamps and his back room to liniments. He says the two trades are the same trade, a few weeks apart.
THE ROOF GARDENS.—The roof gardens of Broadway are open, with music, ices and a breeze. A druggist of Herald square sells a remedy for those who stay up late enough to need one.

THE LIGHT.—The streets of the lower wards are to have the electric light, and the gas men are said to be taking it hard. A druggist of Grand street sells a remedy for the eyes for those not used to seeing the ward clearly.
THE EXCISE BOARD.—The Excise Board has refused licenses to forty saloons of the ward. Several of the forty have taken out licenses as druggists, and are selling the same goods in smaller glasses.
THE MOTOR WAGONS.—A brewery of the East Side has put a motor wagon on the streets, and its horses have been sold to a druggist, who uses them in his advertising as 'restored by the remedy.'
THE TELEPHONE BOOTHS.—A druggist of Grand street has put a telephone booth in his shop, at a nickel the call. He reports that most callers ask the operator for the price of a rival's remedy.

THE MOVING PICTURES.—A moving picture of a patent-medicine show has been taken on the Bowery and is shown in the halls. The lecturer in it says he was not paid, and is asking for a percentage of the remedy.
THE TRUSTS.—The newspapers say there is a trust in everything from beef to ice. The proprietors of the ward, who cannot agree on the price of a cork, deny that there is a trust in remedies.

THE GRAPHOPHONE.—A druggist of Fourteenth street has a talking machine in his window that recites a testimonial every five minutes, in a voice said to be a dead man's. He says it is the same testimonial the man gave living.
THE AEROPLANE.—Two brothers in Ohio are said to have flown in a machine. A proprietor of the ward says his customers have been flying for years, and at a fraction of the cost.
THE BRONX.—The subway to the Bronx is open, and the ward has gone to look at the country. A druggist at the end of the line sells a remedy for hay fever to those who find it.

standing: THE RECIPE.—A woman of Mott street has sold her grandmother's recipe for a cough syrup to a proprietor of the ward for five dollars. The grandmother, who is living, says the recipe was for preserves.

THE TESTIMONIALS.—A proprietor of Canal street has printed a testimonial from a gentleman of Chicago who, on inquiry, lives in Hoboken and has never been to Chicago or taken the remedy. He says he would recommend it, if asked.
THE SAMPLE.—A proprietor of the ward gave away a thousand sample bottles in Hester street on Saturday. Several of the bottles have since been seen for sale in Orchard street, at five cents.

THE LABELS.—A label of a Mulberry street remedy promises relief from forty-one complaints, in type so small that a magnifying glass is given with every bottle. The glass is said to be the more useful.

THE DOSE.—A proprietor was asked by our reporter what the dose of his remedy was. He said a tablespoonful, or a wineglassful in severe cases, or the bottle in very severe cases, and that most cases are very severe.

standing.text: A PRIZE.—A proprietor of the Bowery offers a gold watch to the customer who sends in the most wrappers of his remedy by Christmas. The leader is said to have sent in two hundred, and to be very quiet.

standing: THE CANVASSERS.—Canvassers for a remedy have been going from door to door in Henry street with a book of testimonials and a sample spoon. The tenants report that the spoon is the better made.

THE DEACON.—A deacon of a church in Madison street has signed a testimonial to a bitters, saying that it is no stronger than a strong tea. The temperance ladies of the church have asked him which tea.
A COMPLAINT.—A customer of a remedy of the ward complains that a bottle bought on Monday was green and one bought on Thursday brown. The proprietor says the remedy is seasonal.
THE MARKETS.—Opium firm at the Custom House, the Smyrna crop being short. The proprietors of the ward, who are not supposed to have any interest in the matter, are watching it closely.
THE MARKETS.—Glass bottles up a cent the dozen, corks steady, labels cheap. Proprietors of remedies report the contents, as always, the least of their expenses.

THE BANK BOOK.—A proprietor of the ward has opened an account at a savings bank under another name. The bank says many proprietors do, the remedy business being one in which a man may have to change his name at short notice.
A CLERGYMAN.—A clergyman of the Bowery has refused a hundred dollars for his testimonial to a nerve tonic. The proprietor has raised his offer, and the clergyman his price.

THE ACADEMY.—The Academy of Medicine heard a paper on the patent remedies of the city, with the contents of forty bottles. The paper was not printed, several of the proprietors being subscribers to the Academy's hospital.
THE BARBERS.—A barber of Grand street sells a hair tonic of his own making, and his customers ask him why he is bald. He says that he is the before.

THE STATION HOUSE.—The sergeant at the Elizabeth street station house reports that his men took up eleven men this week who said they had taken nothing but a tonic. He has begun keeping a list of the tonics, which he says is shorter than the list of the men.
THE LOCKSMITH.—A locksmith of Canal street was called to a druggist's on Sunday to open the cellar, the druggist having locked himself in with his stock. He was found in good spirits.
THE GOAT.—A goat of Cherry street ate the label off a bottle of a remedy left on a stoop, and is said to be better for it. The proprietor has used the goat in his advertising, without asking.
THE HAT.—A hatter of the Bowery reports that the proprietors of remedies are his best customers, each ordering a new hat after a good month and the same hat cleaned after a bad one.
THE STOVE.—A woman of Hester street who brewed a remedy of her own on the kitchen stove has been asked by the landlord to stop, and by the neighbors to sell them some.

standing.text: THE CHILDREN'S AID.—The Children's Aid Society has sent a party of the ward's orphans to farms in the West. A proprietor of a tonic has sent a case with them, for the farmers.

standing: THE LECTURE.—A lecturer at a Bowery hall showed the audience a tapeworm in a jar, and sold a remedy for it at the door. Several of the audience who had never had a tapeworm bought two bottles.
THE BOARDING-HOUSE.—A boarding-house of St. Mark's place forbids remedies at table. The boarders take them in the hall, and the landlady says the hall is now the most popular room in the house.

THE JURY.—A juror at the General Sessions asked to be excused, being a proprietor of remedies with a large mail to answer. The Judge excused him, saying the mail was probably more urgent than the case.
THE STABLES.—A veterinary of Elm street sells a liniment for horses which several hackmen have been seen to use on themselves. The veterinary says the dose is the same, and the result.

THE MAYOR'S OFFICE.—The Mayor's marshal has licensed forty new peddlers this month, eleven of them for remedies. The marshal says the remedies are the easiest to license, being the hardest to inspect.

THE PAWN TICKETS.—A pawnbroker of Division street lent a dollar on a bottle of a celebrated tonic, the owner swearing it was worth five. The bottle has not been redeemed, and the pawnbroker is drinking it to find out.
THE STOCK.—A proprietor whose shop burned in Canal street says the fire was put out by the remedy, which ran from the shelves in a flood. The fire marshal says the flood made the fire worse.
A TRIAL.—A peddler accused of selling colored water as a cure was acquitted when his counsel showed that the color was genuine.

THE MORGUE.—The Morgue reports eleven unclaimed this week, and the Department asks the public to come and look. A proprietor of the ward has sent a man to see whether any are customers, and he has reported that it is hard to say.
A REUNION.—The Old Guard of the Sixth Ward dined at a hall in Grand street, and toasted the days when the ward had no doctors, only druggists, and was healthier. The druggists present drank to that.
THE SLEEPERS.—A gentleman who fell asleep in a Bowery barber's chair after taking a remedy for his nerves was shaved, trimmed and shampooed before he woke, and refused to pay for any of it.

standing.text: THE HORSE CARS.—The horse car men of the city have struck for twelve hours a day, and walk the streets with their whips. The druggists sell them a remedy for the feet, which they say is a new experience.
THE GASLIGHT.—The gas company has raised its price, and the druggists of the ward sell more candles and more remedies for the eyes. They report the two trades a natural pair.
THE STREET CLEANERS.—The street-cleaning contractor's men swept Mott street once this month, by the calendar, and are paid for four. The druggists sell a remedy for the dust the once raised.
THE MOTOR CAR.—A druggist of upper Broadway has bought an automobile to deliver his remedy, and the remedy is said to arrive shaken up, which he says is as the label directs.
THE STRIKE.—The subway diggers struck for more pay and the streets above stayed open a week. The druggists of Elm street, whose doors had been in a trench, report the best week of the year.

THE NEW LAW.—The proprietors of the ward have begun to read the labels of their rivals' remedies, to see what will have to be declared. Several have been surprised, and one has been surprised by his own.

THE SUFFRAGISTS.—The ladies of the suffrage society held a meeting at Cooper Union and were heckled from the gallery. A proprietor of a remedy for female complaints sent a box of his pamphlets, which were returned unopened.

THE RADIUM.—A proprietor of the ward who added the word RADIUM to his label has been asked by a physician how much radium is in it. He has answered that there is as much radium in it as there is in the physician's practice.

standingDated.text: THE PEDESTAL FUND.—The World asks a dollar of every reader toward a pedestal for the Statue, which waits in its crates. A proprietor of bitters has offered a hundred dollars if the lady may hold one of his bottles instead of the torch.

GENERAL GRANT.—The General is dead at Mount McGregor, of the cancer in his throat that kept him writing his memoirs to the last. The druggists of the ward report that he took nothing for it but cocaine and a little morphine, and offer both at the usual rates.
THE FUNERAL.—The General's funeral went up Broadway for five hours. The ward is draped in black; a throat lozenge is advertised in his memory at a reduction.
THE PEDESTAL FUND.—The World's subscription has passed a hundred thousand dollars, chiefly in dimes from schoolchildren. The proprietor of bitters has withdrawn his offer and sent a dollar.
JUMBO.—Mr. Barnum's great elephant has been killed by a locomotive in Canada. The druggists of the ward, who had been selling a 'Jumbo Liniment,' have reduced the bottle.
THE PRESIDENT'S WEDDING.—The President has married Miss Folsom at the White House. A proprietor of a tonic has sent the couple a case, and advertised that he did.
THE STATUE.—Liberty is unveiled in the harbor in a fog so thick that the guns could not find her. The ward celebrated with fireworks and a remedy, and some will feel both for a week.
THE ELECTION.—Mr. Henry George, of the single tax, runs for Mayor with the workingmen behind him. A druggist of the Bowery has named a tonic for him, and taxes nothing but the bottle.
THE BLIZZARD.—Snow to the second story in Mulberry street; no cars, no coal, no milk. The druggists alone kept their doors open, and their prices.
THE ELECTION.—The ward voted early and often. A remedy for hoarseness was given away at the polling place, by a candidate who had several.
THE CENTENNIAL.—The city kept the hundredth year of General Washington's inauguration with three days of parades. A druggist on Broad street exhibited the President's false teeth, or a set of them.

THE OTHER HALF.—A police reporter has made a book of the tenements, with photographs taken by flash-light in the rooms at night. The ward has not read it; a druggist of Mulberry street has, and has taken his card out of one of the pictures.
BARNUM.—Mr. Barnum is dead at Bridgeport, the greatest showman of the age. The proprietors of remedies, who learned their trade from him, have put crape on their wagons.
THE ISLAND.—The new immigrant station on Ellis Island is open. Each arrival is examined by a physician; those found sickly are sent back, and the rest are sent to Mulberry street.
THE CHOLERA.—Ships from Hamburg are held at quarantine with cholera aboard. The druggists of the city report a run on every bottle with 'cholera' on the label, and some without.

THE COLUMBIAN PARADE.—The city kept the four hundredth year of Columbus with three days of parades, and the ward turned out under its flags. A druggist of Mulberry street sold a 'Discovery Tonic,' which he says is the first thing Columbus would have bought.
THE PANIC.—The banks are calling in their loans and the mills are shut. The ward has no money for medicine, and buys it anyway, on credit, from a man who has none either.
THE ELECTION.—The reform ticket has beaten the Hall, and the new Mayor promises to clean out the police. The druggists of the ward are waiting to see whether he means it.
THE POLICE BOARD.—Mr. Roosevelt walks the beats at night to catch his patrolmen asleep. He found two in a druggist's doorway, sleeping very soundly, and has asked what the druggist sells.

THE CAMPAIGN.—Mr. Bryan spoke for free silver at the Garden in the heat for two hours, and much of the crowd went home before he did. A proprietor of the ward has put out a Sixteen-to-One Tonic: sixteen parts water to one of the remedy.
THE TOMB.—General Grant's tomb is dedicated on Riverside Drive with a parade of many thousands. The proprietor of bitters who once offered to make up the fund sent a wreath, with his card.
THE FIRE AT ELLIS ISLAND.—The immigrant station has burned to the ground in the night, and the old records with it. Nobody was hurt; the steerage is to land at the Barge Office again.

THE ELECTION.—The Hall has carried the first election of the Greater City, and the ward kept it with bonfires. The druggists sold the remedy for the morning after at the old Manhattan price, the greater city not yet having reached it.
THE GREATER CITY.—Brooklyn, Queens and Staten Island are joined to New York at midnight. The druggists of Brooklyn are now in the same city as their creditors.
THE WAR.—The Maine is sunk in Havana harbor, and the papers are for war. Recruits in the Sixth Ward are offered a tonic 'for the climate of Cuba' at a soldier's discount.
SANTIAGO.—The Spanish fleet is destroyed off Santiago, and the city has surrendered. The druggists of the ward put out flags and a tonic 'for the heroes,' at a hero's price.

MONTAUK.—The soldiers come home from Cuba to the camp at Montauk with the fever, and their families go down to look for them. A proprietor has sent a carload of his tonic; the surgeons have sent it back.
THE DEWEY PARADE.—Admiral Dewey came up the Bay and down Fifth avenue, under an arch of plaster at Madison square. A proprietor of the ward has named a tonic for the Admiral, who has not been asked.

THE AUTOMOBILE SHOW.—Horseless carriages by the hundred, steam, electric and gasoline, are on show at the Garden. The cab horses on the rank outside are said to be taking it hard, and a druggist has advertised a remedy for them.

THE PRESIDENT.—President McKinley is dead at Buffalo of the assassin's bullet, and Mr. Roosevelt is President. A druggist of the Bowery who had advertised a 'Pan-American Tonic' has taken the card out of his window.
THE ELECTION.—The Fusion ticket has beaten the Hall, and Mr. Low is to be Mayor. A tonic called the Reform has been put up in the ward, and is said to be weaker than the old one.
THE ELECTION.—The Hall is back, and Mr. McClellan is Mayor. The druggists of the ward have taken the Reform tonic off the shelf, where it had not been disturbed.

THE SLOCUM.—The excursion steamer General Slocum burned in the East River with the Sunday school of a German church aboard, and more than a thousand are dead, most of them women and children. The life preservers were rotten, and some, it is said, had iron in them to make up the weight. The ward knows something of what is sold under a label, and is in mourning with Little Germany.

THE SUBWAY.—The underground railway is open from City Hall to Harlem in fifteen minutes. A tonic for the nerves of passengers is sold at every station but the first, whose passengers have not yet been down.
THE MAGAZINES.—Collier's prints 'The Great American Fraud,' naming the remedies and what is in them. The druggists of the ward report the article is very popular, and so, still, are the remedies.

THE CHAMPIONSHIP.—The Giants have beaten the Athletics of Philadelphia for the championship of the world, Mathewson pitching three games and giving up no run in any of them. A proprietor of the ward has named a liniment for his arm, without asking.

THE ELECTION.—Mr. Hearst ran for Mayor against the Hall and very nearly beat it, and the count is disputed. A proprietor of a nerve tonic who advertised in both camps reports a good result either way.
THE PACKING HOUSES.—A novel of the Chicago stockyards has put the city off its sausage. The proprietors of remedies, whose own works have not yet been written up, are reading it with great attention.
SAN FRANCISCO.—The city is shaken down and burned. A proprietor of the ward has sent a case of his remedy to the relief committee, which has asked him to send money instead.

THE MUCK-RAKERS.—The President says the magazine writers who expose the trusts are like the man with the muck-rake, who could look no way but down. The proprietors of the ward agree, and wish the writers would look the other way altogether.
THE PURE FOOD LAW.—Congress has passed, and the President signed, a law that every bottle shall say upon its label what is in it, from the first of January. The trade has six months to find out.

verdictLead: The bottle found at the bedside bore the label of {label}. Whether its proprietor spoke for his preparations or kept away, it did not detain the jury long. Physicians observe that the remedy is purely vegetable, and that so is hemlock.

verdictLead.text: A chemist from the College of Pharmacy gave evidence that the bottle of {label} contained, besides syrup and spirit, enough of a certain drug to quiet a dray-horse. The proprietor's advertisements describe it as gentle.

verdictLead: The jury retired for twenty minutes and returned with the label of {label} written into its verdict. The foreman remarked that he had a bottle of it at home, and would be pouring it away.
The bottle of {label} was passed along the jury, and each man smelled it. The foreman said afterward that the smell was evidence enough, and the chemist's report only confirmed it.

IN THE TRADE.—The proprietor's almanac for the year is out, with the tides, the eclipses, a page of jokes and the claims of {product}, of which the jokes are said to be the most believed.
IN THE TRADE.—A new almanac of {product} is to be had free at the shop and by post, with a calendar, a dream book and forty testimonials. The dream book is said to be the most accurate part.

IN THE TRADE.—The almanac of {product} is printed again, ten thousand strong, with the Saints' days, the phases of the moon and the remedy for each. The printer of Ann street says it is his best seller after the Bible.
investmentNotices.wholesale_contract.bought: IN THE TRADE.—Messrs. Kittredge & Vail of Newark will take the goods of {product} by the dozen, for druggists in Paterson, Newark and Elizabeth. New Jersey is to be cured wholesale.
investmentNotices.laboratory.bought: IN THE TRADE.—A back room on Mulberry street has been fitted with retorts, and a German chemist installed who asks no questions. The neighbors have begun to ask some.
almanac.lapsed: IN THE TRADE.—The proprietor's almanac for the year is out of date, and is now chiefly used for lighting fires. It may be had again on application.
IN THE TRADE.—The year's almanac of {product} has run its course, and its predictions with it. The kitchens of the ward are said to be using it for curl-papers.
IN THE TRADE.—The almanac of {product} has had its year, and the last copies hang on nails in the privies of the ward, where they are read more closely than anywhere else.
investmentNotices.branch_shop.lost: IN THE TRADE.—The branch in the Ninth Ward has put up its shutters. The clerk is said to have taken the till, and the ward to have taken the clerk's side.
investmentNotices.wholesale_contract.lost: IN THE TRADE.—Messrs. Kittredge & Vail of Newark have cancelled their order for {product}, having read the papers. New Jersey will have to find its own remedies.
laboratory.mishap: FIRE.—A blaze in a back room on Mulberry street brought out Engine No. 9 on {weekday}. A quantity of ether was found to be the cause, and a German chemist the excuse. The proprietor's loss is put at twenty-five dollars, and the talk at a good deal more.

FIRE.—The laboratory behind the shop on Mulberry street took fire on {weekday} when a retort cracked over the gas. The chemist put it out with a wet sack; the loss is put at twenty-five dollars and the chemist's eyebrows.

FIRE.—Smoke was seen from the back of the shop on Mulberry street on {weekday}, and the engines came. The proprietor says it was an experiment; the neighbors that it was a fire; the loss, of twenty-five dollars, says the neighbors were right.

FIRE.—An explosion in the laboratory behind the shop on Mulberry street broke two windows on {weekday} and frightened a horse. The chemist is unhurt and says he has learned something; the loss is twenty-five dollars.
investmentNotices.druggists_order.bought: IN THE TRADE.—A druggist of Atlantic avenue, Brooklyn, is to keep {product} on his own shelf, a dozen or so at a time. He describes it to our reporter as a remedy of the highest character, and the price he pays for it as none of our business.
investmentNotices.druggists_order.lost: IN THE TRADE.—The Atlantic avenue druggist has sent back the last of {product}, saying he has a family name to think of. He has taken a rival's bitters in its place.
investmentNotices.larger_copper.bought: IN THE TRADE.—The coppersmith of Elm street has delivered a larger copper to the shop on Mulberry street, with a worm long enough, he says, to run round the block. Each still will now fill half as many bottles again; the ward has been asked to keep its windows shut.
investmentNotices.fourth_still.bought: IN THE TRADE.—A fourth still has gone into the back of the shop on Mulberry street, and the neighbors report that the floor above is warm in January. The proprietor speaks of a manufactory.

outOfTown: OUT OF TOWN.—A death at Paterson is laid by the family to a remedy bought from a druggist there. The druggist says he had it by the dozen from New-York, and is sorry.
OUT OF TOWN.—The Newark papers report a death from a patent medicine sold over a counter in Market street. The bottle came from New-York, by the gross.
OUT OF TOWN.—At Yonkers, a coroner's jury has found that a laborer died of a remedy he did not know the name of. Nor, it is said, did the druggist who sold it.
OUT OF TOWN.—At Elizabeth, N. J., a death is reported of a man who took a patent remedy bought of a druggist there. The druggist had it from New-York, and will have no more.
OUT OF TOWN.—The Paterson coroner sat upon a millhand who had been dosing himself with a remedy from New-York. The jury could not agree on the remedy, but agreed on New-York.

tails: A passenger who took a remedy for sea-sickness at Queenstown reports that it made him forget the sea entirely, and much else.
The purser reports a quiet passage. The ship's surgeon reports the same, having sold out his stock of a tonic by the third day.
A case consigned to a druggist of Grand street, marked GLASS, was found on inspection to be marked correctly.
The {ship}'s captain reports fog off the Banks, and a passenger who sold remedies in the saloon until the purser locked them up.
A cabin passenger is said to be a celebrated physician from Vienna. The proprietors of the city have sent cards to his hotel.
In the {ship}'s hold, eleven hundred bags of coffee and two cases of a French elixir, which the Customs have kept for further tasting.
The {ship2}'s steerage included a family of eleven, all well, which the druggists of the ward regard as a challenge.
